analysis.one_liner: Makes executives at big banks personally certify their firm is free of unreported fraud, backed by prison time.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote: it died in committee with zero cosponsors in the 2017-2019 Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would turn the temporary bailout watchdog SIGTARP into a permanent office whose sole job is investigating fraud at banks, bank holding companies, and savings-and-loan holding companies [S2][S3]. The four top officers of any such firm with over $10 billion in assets would have to certify each year that they checked for criminal conduct or civil fraud and disclosed anything they found, facing fines and up to five years in prison for a false or missing certification — ten years in a pattern involving more than $100,000 [S3]. It would also require a court to find that any corporate deferred-prosecution agreement — the settlements that let companies avoid criminal conviction — serves the public interest, and require the Justice Department to post those agreements and their monitor terms online [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary depositors, taxpayers, and communities that absorb the damage when banks commit fraud and get settlements instead of prosecutions. The bill's own findings note the existing watchdog's work produced criminal charges against more than 400 defendants, including nearly 100 bankers, tied to failed banks with an estimated $7 billion loss to the deposit insurance fund [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Creates a permanent, dedicated law-enforcement office for financial-institution fraud by redesignating SIGTARP as the Office of the Special Inspector General for Financial Institution Crime, ending its scheduled shutdown with the TARP wind-down [S2][S3].

Requires the CEO, CFO, COO, and chief compliance officer of any financial institution or holding company over $10 billion in assets to certify annually that they performed due diligence for criminal conduct or civil fraud and disclosed all of it to the Justice Department or their regulator, with criminal penalties of up to five years for willful violations and up to ten years for violations as part of a pattern involving more than $100,000 [S3].

Requires a federal court to approve a corporate deferred-prosecution agreement only if it finds the deal is in the public interest — weighing whether required reforms will prevent repeat misconduct and whether penalties compensate victims — and blocks approval of repeat-offender deals without good cause [S3].

Requires the Justice Department to post the text of corporate deferred-prosecution agreements and the terms of the monitors who oversee them, ending secret settlements, and gives the Special Inspector General authority over which regulator records can be withheld from it, including the bank-examiner privilege [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Executives at large banks and their companies, who would face personal legal exposure, compliance costs to run the required due-diligence process, and public court review of their settlement deals with the government. Banks above $10 billion in assets are covered; smaller banks are not [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Executives and big banks over $10B in assets

drawbacks.text: Annual certifications that 'no undisclosed criminal conduct exists' are hard to make honestly — a top officer cannot truly vouch for every branch and subsidiary — so the requirement could produce either box-checking compliance or defensive over-disclosure, without directly stopping the underlying fraud [S3].

Large banks would bear new compliance and legal costs for the annual certification process and possible civil penalties (up to $25,000 per willful violation, $500 for negligent ones), costs that are passed through to customers and shareholders like any compliance expense [S3].

Adding a permanent fraud watchdog alongside the Justice Department, the SEC, and the banking regulators raises the risk of duplicated investigations and coordination overhead, even though the bill requires the office to coordinate with those agencies' inspectors general [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The compliance costs are real but small against the scale of losses the bill targets — its own findings tie SIGTARP's past work to charges against nearly 100 bankers and about $7 billion in losses to the deposit insurance fund at failed banks [S3]. The executive-certification mechanism is the weakest part, since it relies on officers' own diligence; the stronger teeth are the permanent investigative office, the ban on secret settlement terms, and court review of repeat-offender deals. On balance it is a targeted accountability measure, though whether certifications change behavior is a fair doubt.

outcome.mechanism: Elizabeth Warren introduced it in March 2018 and the Senate Banking Committee never acted on it; it expired with the Congress in January 2019 without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 14, 2018, read twice, and referred to the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, which was its last action of record [S1][S5].
No other senator cosponsored the bill — the cosponsor list is zero [S4].

The bill's findings built its case on SIGTARP's record: criminal charges against more than 400 defendants including nearly 100 bankers, and Justice Department actions against 10 financial institutions, 8 of them with assets over $100 billion [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large banks and their top executives, who avoided an annual certification duty carrying prison exposure, a permanent fraud-investigation office, and public court review of their deferred-prosecution deals.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big banks and their top executives

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Senate Banking Committee; no senator joined as a cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.role: Committee of referral for banking bills
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors from either party, so the record shows only that a single Democrat sponsored the bill and no senator of either party signed on.

industries.industry: Large banks, bank holding companies, and savings-and-loan holding companies (over $10B in assets)
industries.note: The bill would impose annual executive certifications for fraud, create a permanent office dedicated to investigating fraud at these firms, and strip regulators' ability to withhold records from that office. The firms' interest in avoiding prosecution-level accountability runs against depositors and taxpayers who absorb fraud losses.

industries.industry: Corporations that settle federal charges through deferred-prosecution agreements
industries.note: The bill's court-review amendment would open settlement deals with the Justice Department to a public-interest determination and mandatory publication of the agreement and monitor terms. Companies that rely on these deals to avoid criminal conviction lose negotiating privacy and leverage.

industries.industry: Bank compliance and legal functions at large firms
industries.note: The annual certification duty would create a permanent due-diligence workflow for the four top officers of every covered firm. Compliance and legal staff gain responsibilities and headcount, a cost banks would bear.
